text: Following last lesson's diagnosis, you now have a decision to make: re-run with a fix, or stop and report what you have. This lesson is about making that decision deliberately, using the cut list you wrote earlier, rather than drifting into either endless re-runs or giving up prematurely.

This lesson covers how to decide, concretely, whether an iteration is worth the remaining time budget, the difference between a targeted re-run and an open-ended 'try again and hope' re-run, how to update your run log and analysis cleanly when you do iterate, and a worked iteration decision continuing the running capstone.

Go back to your cut list and time budget before deciding to re-run anything. A re-run is worth doing when it's targeted — you've identified a specific, fixable confound, not a vague 'let's see if it looks different' — when it fits inside your remaining time budget including its own queue time, and when it would meaningfully change what you can honestly conclude.

A targeted re-run changes exactly one thing based on a specific diagnosis — in the running example, re-submitting both qubit counts within the same short window specifically to close the calibration-window gap, with everything else held fixed. An open-ended re-run, without a specific hypothesis about what changed, risks burning your remaining time without resolving the ambiguity. When you do iterate, keep the original run's data and log entry rather than overwriting it, and add the new run as a new, clearly labeled entry — you may end up citing both in your eventual report.

In the worked decision: the cut list didn't anticipate this specific calibration-window confound, so check the remaining time budget directly against the run log's recorded queue-wait times for the first attempt. If a same-window interleaved re-run fits before write-up needs to start, it's a good candidate. If it doesn't fit, the honest fallback — reporting the original result with the confound explicitly named — is the right call, not a lesser one.
Next lesson closes out Chapter 4: the point where you stop running jobs and deliberately lock down exactly what data and analysis will go into the report and presentation.
